title: The top of the pole
hook: how do you step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole? (Gateless Gate 46)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhaozhou's answer: the cypress tree in front of the garden. Your line: the cypress in the garden. Which tree did you look at, and for how long before the mind moved on? Day one thousand two hundred forty-six, and the week closes.

Look back at this week. It opened with Dogen telling us how to sit, and then said the blue mountains are walking. Then the koans came, one a day. A man hanging from a branch by his teeth. A monk calling his own name and answering yes. Three pounds of flax. A cypress tree in a courtyard. Each one took away somewhere to stand: no safe answer, no faraway meaning. Today's case goes all the way up. A teacher named Shishuang asks: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you take one step forward?
screen: `DOGEN: SIT. THE MOUNTAINS WALK.` → `TEETH, A NAME, FLAX, A TREE.` → `NOW: A HUNDRED-FOOT POLE.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. A pole, a hundred feet high, and someone who has climbed it all the way. That took effort. Every hand over hand was real work. Now they're at the top, balanced, with the whole sky around them. And Shishuang's question isn't how did you get here. It's how do you step forward from here. There's no more pole to climb. Second, the old teacher's warning. The case adds the words of another teacher from long before. In paraphrase: someone sitting on top of the hundred-foot pole has got somewhere, but it isn't yet the real thing. They need to take one more step, and show their whole body in all ten directions. Third, why the top can be a trap. Some teachers read the top of the pole as an attainment you can hold onto: a calm you finally reached, a breakthrough in sitting, a self-image as someone who gets it. It feels like arriving. The case says arriving is where you get stuck. Stepping off doesn't mean throwing your practice away. Some readers hear it as letting go of the height itself, coming back down into the whole world, all ten directions, ordinary life included. Fourth, how this fits the week. The flax and the cypress both said: it's right here, nothing far away. The pole says the same thing from the other side. Even something you reached by climbing becomes a new place to cling. The koan asks for one more step, and leaves the stepping to you.
screen: `A HUNDRED-FOOT POLE, CLIMBED.` · `ONE MORE STEP, IN ALL DIRECTIONS.` · `THE TOP CAN BE A TRAP.` · `THE FLAX, THE TREE, THE POLE.` · then, large: `STEP OFF THE POLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and settle with the breath. Think of one place you've climbed to and now hold tightly: a routine, a way of being seen, a comfort you guard. Don't judge it. Just notice how your body holds it, the grip in the shoulders or the jaw. Then, on an out-breath, picture loosening that grip by a single degree. One small step past comfort, not a leap. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The top of the pole. Shishuang's question in case forty-six of the Gateless Gate: from the top of a hundred-foot pole, how do you step forward? Today's word.
screen: `THE TOP OF THE POLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: step off the pole. Today, find one small thing just past your comfort, a call you've put off or a new way home, and take that single step. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen this case is given as a koan, and teachers sometimes use the image of the pole's top to warn students against holding on to a calm or insight they have reached in sitting.

notes: Week-end day (1246): the hook looks back over days 1240–1245. Days 1240 and 1241 were not on disk; the look-back uses their index (Dogen's instructions for sitting; the mountains walking).

Case 46 paraphrased. Confirm: Shishuang (Sekiso) asks how to step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole; an earlier teacher (often identified as Changsha) says one sitting atop the pole has entered but not yet truly, and must step forward to manifest the whole body in the ten directions. The earlier teacher is left unnamed in the script.
Reading the pole's top as an attainment one clings to is presented as a common reading ('often read'); confirm.
Original 百尺竿頭: confirm characters and pronunciation.
Editor pass: softened 'often read' and 'readers often hear' to 'some teachers' and 'some readers'.
